source_text: Quod etiam in ipso fumi principe inmanitatem solam aduertisti, quam uituperares, nonne debuisti adtendere cetera, quae te in eius naturae laudem cogerent? habebat enim animam et corpus, illam uiuificantem, hoc uita inspiratum, cum illa regeret, hoc obtemperaret; illa praeiret, hoc subsequeretur; illa contineret, hoc non difflueret; illa moueret in numeros, hoc numerosa membrorum conpagine constabiliretur. nonne te ad laudem mouet in hoc uno principe uel pax ordinata uel ordo pacatus? quod autem de uno dictum est, hoc de * ceteris intellegi licet. sed enim erat in alios ferus et inmanis. non hoc laudo, sed tanta illa, quae non uis adtendere. quae si uel admonitus intuetur atque considerat, quisquis Manichaeo temere credidit, sine dubitatione cognoscit, cum de istis naturis loquitur, de bonis quibusdam se loqui, sed non summis et infabricatis, sicuti est deus una trinitas, neque de his fabricatis, quae sublimiter ordinata sunt, sicuti sunt angeli sancti et beatissimae potestates, sed de infimis et pro sui generis modulo in imo rerum ordinatis bonis: quae dum conparantur superioribus, uituperandae ab inperitis existimantur, et dum consideratur, quantum his desit boni, quod illis adest, eiusdem boni absentia mali nomen tenet. et ego quidem propterea sic de istis naturis disputo, quoniam ea nominantur, quae in hoc mundo nota nobis sunt. nouimus enim tenebras, aquas, uentos, ignem, fumum; nouimus etiam animalia serpentia, natantia, uolantia, quadrupedia, bipedia: in quibus. omnibus exceptis tenebris, quae, ut dixi, nihil sunt aliud quam lucis absentia, quae oculis non uidendo discernuntur — sicut silentium auribus non audiendo — non quia tenebrae sunt aliquid, sed quia lux non est — sicut non quia silentium est aliquid, sed quia sonus non est — exceptis ergo tenebris in hac enumeratione ceterae naturae sunt et omnibus notae, quarum speciem, quia, in quantumcumque est, laudabilis et bona est, nemo prudens abalienat ab auctore omnium bonorum deo.
thought_title: The prince of smoke also shows ordered good
orientation: Augustine is speaking, pressing his argument that every nature insofar as it exists is good by examining Mani's prince of smoke.
pass_a_gloss: Although you noticed in the very prince of smoke only the monstrousness, which you might blame, ought you not to have attended to the rest, which would compel you to praise of his nature? For he had soul and body, the one making alive, the other breathed into with life, while the one ruled, the other obeyed; the one went first, the other followed; the one held together, the other did not flow apart; the one moved into measures, the other was made firm by a measured framework of limbs. Does either ordered peace or peaceful order in this one prince not move you to praise? But what has been said concerning one, it is permitted to be understood concerning the rest. But he was savage and monstrous toward others. I do not praise this, but those so great things, which you do not wish to attend to. Which things if, even when reminded, whoever believed Mani rashly looks at and considers, he knows without hesitation that when he speaks about these natures he speaks about certain good things, but not about highest and unmade things, just as God one Trinity is, nor about made things which have been ordered on high, just as the holy angels and the most blessed powers are, but about lowest good things ordered at the bottom of things according to the measure of their own kind: which, while they are compared to higher things, are thought by the unskilled to deserve blame, and while it is considered how much of good is lacking to these, which is present to those, the absence of the same good holds the name of evil. And I indeed for this reason argue thus about these natures, because those things are named which are known to us in this world. For we know darkness, waters, winds, fire, smoke; we know also creeping animals, swimming, flying, four-footed, two-footed: among which in all things with darkness excepted, which, as I said, are nothing else than absence of light, which are discerned by eyes by not seeing - just as silence is discerned by ears by not hearing - not because darkness is something, but because light is not - just as not because silence is something, but because sound is not - with darkness therefore excepted in this listing the remaining natures both are and are known to all, whose form, because to whatever extent it is it is praiseworthy and good, no wise man separates from God the author of all good things.

choices.why: brief glossary fixes natura as nature
brief glossary fixes species as form in the sense of beauty of a thing
brief names map Manichaeus to Mani
keeps the chiasmus and the force of ordered versus peaceful without adding nouns

pass_b_english: Even in that prince of smoke himself you noticed only one thing. You saw his monstrousness, so you could condemn him. Should you not have looked at all the rest? It would have forced you to praise his nature. He had a soul and a body. The soul gave life, and the body breathed with that life. The soul ruled, and the body obeyed. The soul led, and the body followed. The soul held him together, and the body did not fall apart. The soul moved in rhythm, and the body stood firm in the joined frame of its many limbs. Does the ordered peace or the peaceful order in this one prince not move you to praise?

What I have said of this one prince holds for all the rest. He was savage and monstrous toward others. I do not praise that. I praise all those great goods you refuse to notice. Anyone who believed Mani without thinking should look at those goods now, even if he needs prompting. If he looks and weighs them, he will know without doubt what he is speaking of. When he speaks of these natures, he speaks of certain good things. They are not the highest and unmade goods, as God is, one Trinity. They are not made goods set high in the order, as the holy angels and the most blessed powers are. They are the lowest goods, set at the bottom of things in the measure proper to their kind.

The unskilled condemn them only because they compare them with higher things. They see how much good these lower things lack, a good the higher things possess. They give the name of evil to the absence of that same good. I speak of these natures in this way for one reason. Mani names things we already know in this world. We know darkness and waters and winds and fire and smoke. We also know crawling animals and swimming and flying animals, and four-footed and two-footed animals. Take darkness out of that list. Darkness is nothing but the absence of light, as I have said. The eye tells it apart by not seeing, as the ear tells silence apart by not hearing. That is not because darkness is something, but because light is absent, just as it is not because silence is something, but because sound is absent. Apart from darkness, all the rest in that list are natures, and everyone knows them. Their form is praiseworthy and good in whatever measure it exists. No wise person separates that form from God, the author of all good things.
notes: source has * before ceteris, apparently an editorial mark, glossed as the rest
source punctuation in quibus. omnibus appears broken, glossed as among which in all things

problems.quote: It counts because light is absent, not because darkness is something. Silence counts because sound is absent, not because silence is something.
problems.source_quote: non quia tenebrae sunt aliquid, sed quia lux non est — sicut non quia silentium est aliquid, sed quia sonus non est
problems.why: The clause explains how darkness and silence are discerned, not that they 'count' or matter.
problems.fix: Not because darkness is something, but because light is not there; not because silence is something, but because sound is not.
problems.ruling: Source 'oculis non uidendo discernuntur... non quia tenebrae sunt aliquid, sed quia lux non est' explains discernment; 'counts' is an unsupported mistranslation that misleads.

edits.old: It counts because light is absent, not because darkness is something. Silence counts because sound is absent, not because silence is something.
edits.new: That is not because darkness is something, but because light is absent, just as it is not because silence is something, but because sound is absent.

fixed: Fixed `It counts / Silence counts` to `not because... but because...` to match source `non quia tenebrae sunt aliquid, sed quia lux non est — sicut non quia silentium est aliquid, sed quia sonus non est`.

problems.quote: Does that ordered peace not move you to praise him? Does that peaceful order in this one prince not move you?
problems.source_quote: nonne te ad laudem mouet in hoc uno principe uel pax ordinata uel ordo pacatus?
problems.why: The single question is duplicated, and 'ordered peace' vs 'peaceful order' are the two alternatives (uel...uel), which the doubling obscures; 'or' is lost.
problems.fix: Does neither the ordered peace nor the peaceful order in this one prince move you to praise?
problems.ruling: One question, uel pax ordinata uel ordo pacatus, is split in two and the 'or' is lost.

edits.old: Does that ordered peace not move you to praise him? Does that peaceful order in this one prince not move you?
edits.new: Does the ordered peace or the peaceful order in this one prince not move you to praise?

fixed: Merged duplicated question into one question with 'or' for uel pax ordinata uel ordo pacatus.

last_rejected.quote: They see how much good these lower things lack, a good the higher things possess. They give the name of evil to the absence of that same good.
last_rejected.source_quote: dum consideratur, quantum his desit boni, quod illis adest, eiusdem boni absentia mali nomen tenet.
last_rejected.why: The absence itself bears the name evil; the unskilled are not the ones who name it.
last_rejected.fix: When one considers how much good these lower things lack, which the higher possess, the absence of that same good bears the name of evil.
last_rejected.ruling: Source 'uituperandae ab inperitis existimantur' precedes; 'absentia mali nomen tenet' is impersonal, but English attributing naming to the unskilled is a minor, contextually consistent reading, not meaning-changing.

last_rejected.quote: Mani names things we already know in this world.
last_rejected.source_quote: quoniam ea nominantur, quae in hoc mundo nota nobis sunt
last_rejected.why: Source has impersonal 'ea nominantur' (those things are named); English attributes naming to Mani, which is an addition, though plausible. Minor shift of agency.
last_rejected.fix: I speak of these natures in this way because the things named are ones known to us in this world.
last_rejected.ruling: “ea nominantur, quae…nota nobis sunt” stays: named things are familiar. Supplying Mani from context is only an agency shift.

last_rejected.quote: The soul moved in rhythm, and the body stood firm in the joined frame of its many limbs.
last_rejected.source_quote: illa moueret in numeros, hoc numerosa membrorum conpagine constabiliretur
last_rejected.why: 'Moueret in numeros' means the soul set the body moving in measured rhythm; the body was steadied by the numerous joining of limbs. English loses causation.
last_rejected.fix: The soul set it moving in measured rhythm, and the body was held steady by the well-ordered joining of its limbs.
last_rejected.ruling: “moueret in numeros” means moved in rhythm; “constabiliretur” still shows the body held firm by “membrorum conpagine.” No major loss.
